You might want to ask yourself what is on the other side of all that allegedly terrifying government “debt”.
A government's liability is somebody else's asset.
Those Treasury securities aren't $40 trillion that disappeared down a hole. They are dollar-denominated financial assets held by pension funds, banks, businesses, households, foreign institutions and other parts of the financial system. As Stephanie Kelton puts the basic accounting point: the government's red ink is somebody else's black ink.
And where do you imagine government spending actually goes?
Into the private economy: paying companies supplying the government, public sector workers, defence contractors, pensioners, infrastructure workers, researchers and millions of others. It builds roads, pays Social Security, funds Medicare, supports universities and research, purchases military equipment and pays interest to holders of government securities.
The United States is not an “over-extended borrower” of dollars in the sense that you or I can become over-extended borrowers of dollars.
It is the issuer of the dollar.

That doesn't mean deficits can be unlimited. Spend beyond the economy's productive capacity and you can get inflation, currency depreciation and serious resource misallocation. Those are real constraints.

But “$40 trillion! The party must be over!” confuses the issuer of the currency with a household using it. If the US government actually eliminated its liabilities, somebody else would necessarily lose the corresponding dollar assets.

Before cheering the disappearance of the government's red ink, you might want to check how much of your own financial system - and how many of the services, incomes and institutions you depend upon - are written on the other side of the ledger.

text:
There is a real story here. Unfortunately, “Every Bond Market in the World Is Breaking” isn't quite it. 
Long-term sovereign yields have risen sharply. Inflation risk, geopolitical shocks, enormous bond issuance, changing investor demand and higher term premia are all important. Higher yields feed into mortgages, corporate borrowing and financial conditions. None of this is trivial. 
 
But falling bond prices are not evidence that bond markets are “breaking”. 
The Bank of England's July Financial Stability Report says explicitly that, despite high volatility, UK gilt and repo markets have remained resilient, with liquidity conditions commensurate with market conditions. Its Monetary Policy Report similarly says the gilt market continues to function in an orderly manner. 
 
More importantly, the oft rehearsed story that governments must continually persuade bondholders to “lend them the money” imports household economics into a monetary system where it doesn't belong. 
Britain issues sterling. America issues dollars. Japan issues yen. They cannot involuntarily run out of currencies they themselves issue in the way a household, company or foreign-currency borrower can. Bond investors can demand higher yields, sell government securities and move currencies. Those actions can affect exchange rates, inflation and financial conditions enormously. 
What they cannot do is deprive the US government of dollars or the British government of sterling. 
 
Nor do rising yields simply mean investors suddenly doubt governments will “repay their debts”. Long-term yields incorporate expected future policy rates and term premia. The Bank estimates that of the roughly 350-basis-point rise in 10-year gilt yields between February 2022 and June 2026, about 200 basis points reflected higher term premia, themselves driven by several factors including changing pension-fund demand, global uncertainty and high government-bond issuance. 
 
And here is the irony: the genuinely dangerous part of a bond sell-off may not be sovereign “insolvency” at all. 
 
Britain demonstrated that spectacularly in 2022. The gilt sell-off became a systemic emergency because leveraged LDI pension strategies faced collateral calls and forced selling. The sovereign wasn't running out of sterling. Private financial leverage was turning falling government-bond prices into a fire sale. 
 
That is where a Steve Keen-style analysis becomes considerably more useful. Ask who created the credit, who is leveraged, whose balance sheets are deteriorating and where forced deleveraging might occur. 
Bond markets matter enormously. But the notion that “yields are rising, therefore governments are running out of lenders” is not sophisticated bond-market analysis. 
 
It is the household analogy wearing a Bloomberg terminal.

There is something faintly nostalgic now about these periodic warnings that Britain is being “punished by the markets”. You can almost hear the rustle of yellowing Treasury briefing papers from the 1970s, dusted off and recirculated for another generation of commentators raised to believe that the British state survives only by the grace of anonymous bond traders somewhere in the City, New York or Singapore.

The names change. The phrases are updated. “Investor confidence”, “credibility”, “bond vigilantes”, “market discipline”. Yet the underlying worldview remains stubbornly intact, preserved like an Edwardian steam engine still ceremonially operated long after electrification made it obsolete.

The Bretton Woods fixed exchange rate theory applied to modern money is interesting not so much for what it explains, but for what it unconsciously reveals. The central contradiction sits almost openly on the page. Britain, we are told, cannot technically default because it issues its own currency. Yet we are also told that crediting pounds to settle obligations would somehow constitute “default by another name".

This is the peculiar metaphysics of modern economic commentary. Payment is simultaneously possible and impossible. The issuer of sterling can always make sterling payments, but is said to be financially constrained in much the same way as a household or corporation that cannot hand over the thing it owes. The contradiction is never resolved because confronting it would collapse the entire moral architecture surrounding public debt.

As MMT economists have proved  in several books now. The operational reality is far, far duller than the drama requires. The British government spends through instructions authorised by Parliament and settled via the Bank of England. Gilt issuance does not provide the state with pounds it otherwise lacks. The pounds necessarily appear first within the banking system before they can be exchanged for government securities afterwards, with redemption merely reversing that exchange at maturity. Bond sales are therefore better understood as an interest rate maintenance operation and a reserve drain than as a funding necessity.

This was once reasonably well understood inside government institutions. One suspects it still is, at least in the quieter corners where settlement systems actually have to function. But public discourse operates according to a different requirement. The state must continually be depicted as financially dependent upon “the markets”, because that framing imposes a useful discipline on democratic ambition.

Hence the endless invocation of “borrowing costs”, as though Britain were a precarious provincial authority begging for overdraft extensions rather than the monopoly issuer of sterling liabilities. The country is described as “paying more to borrow” in the same way medieval theologians once described storms as divine displeasure. Markets become an anthropomorphic force expressing moral judgement upon insufficiently virtuous governments.

We are nothing like a Eurozone country that can no longer issue it's own currency, we don't peg to a scarce resource or hold any foreign debt.
